title: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
content:
Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.
"Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.

- Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
- A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."
The ads Cuban says Meta waves through
Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.
"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.
Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.
What Meta's documents showed
On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.
In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.
Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.

report.summary: Mark Cuban says Meta knowingly runs AI deepfake ads scamming users, while Reuters-reported internal docs estimate scam and prohibited ads brought ~$16B, about 10% of 2024 revenue.
report.background: AI-generated deepfakes of celebrities and executives have become a recurring vehicle for fraud on social platforms. Scammers clone a trusted face and voice, buy ads, and push fake cures, investment schemes, or prohibited products to broad audiences. The economics favor scale: ad systems optimize for engagement and revenue, while moderation must catch millions of creatives in near real time. Cuban is a frequent target because he is a well-known investor and co-founder of Cost Plus Drugs, making a fake diabetes cure pitch plausible to some users. The Reuters-reported documents add a financial dimension: Meta allegedly expected roughly $16 billion, about 10% of 2024 revenue, from ads for scams and prohibited products, and its safety staff estimated its platforms play a role in a third of successful U.S. scams. Meta disputes the characterization.
key_points: Cuban says he receives weekly emails from older users asking about a $294 diabetes cure he never sold. He says the ads use an AI clone of his face and voice, and some include disclaimers that the clip is AI-generated entertainment—but by then, he argues, the pitch has already worked.

Reuters-reported internal Meta documents estimate about $16 billion, or roughly 10% of 2024 revenue, came from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta’s internal count, users saw some 15 billion “higher risk” ads per day, with one late-2024 document valuing that category at about $7 billion a year.

Meta’s automated systems must judge an advertiser at least 95% likely to be running a scam before banning it, according to the documents. Below that threshold, suspected scammers can simply pay more per ad and stay live—a detail Cuban cites as evidence of tolerated harm.

Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents “present a selective view” and called the 10% estimate “rough and overly-inclusive.” He said user complaints about scam ads fell 58% over 18 months and Meta removed more than 134 million scam ads in 2025; the documents also note an SEC inquiry into ads tied to financial fraud.
report.impact: The report shifts the debate from “bad actors exploit platforms” to whether ad systems economically benefit from insufficient enforcement. For AI companies, it raises liability and trust questions: deepfake detection, content provenance, advertiser identity checks, and watermarking may become competitive necessities rather than optional safety features. Developers building generative media tools should expect pressure to embed provenance and misuse controls. For regular users, the practical lesson is that a familiar face and voice in an ad are no longer proof of endorsement—especially for health cures and investments. Regulators may use the revenue estimates to argue that platform incentives, not just moderation budgets, need structural change.
report.tools: Follow Meta Ad Library for ad transparency, C2PA Content Credentials for media provenance, and open-source deepfake detection projects such as DeepfakeBench and FaceForensics++ for research. Report suspected scams to the platform and to FTC/IC3. Browser ad blockers reduce exposure but do not verify legitimacy.
